lessons.title: The new kickoff
lessons.objective: You can explain the dynamic kickoff in one sentence.

payload.prompt: Where does the receiving team line up on the new kickoff?

diagram.alt: Football field showing the new kickoff setup, with the kicking team at the opponent's 40 and the receiving team at their own 35.

explanation.correct: The new dynamic kickoff puts the receiving team at the 35-yard line, ready to return. This change in 2025 opened up more return opportunities and made the game more exciting.
explanation.incorrect: The kicking team lines up at the opponent's 40. The receiving team starts at their own 35-yard line on the new kickoff.
explanation.sayThisLine: The receiving team starts at the 35 on the new kickoff.

payload.prompt: Why did the NFL change the kickoff in 2024?

options.text: To create more exciting returns and reduce short fields
To make the kicker more valuable
Because fans complained about touchbacks

explanation.correct: The dynamic kickoff was designed to bring back more returns and make the play safer by spreading out the collision zone. It worked: touchbacks dropped and returns rose.
explanation.incorrect: The dynamic kickoff was meant to fix the boring touchback problem. Placing the kicking team at the opponent's 40 and the receiving team at their 35 created more room to return.

payload.prompt: Returner catches the ball at the 38-yard line and is tackled at the 45.

scene.alt: A football play showing a kickoff return from the 38 to the 45-yard line.

explanation.correct: The returner caught it in the field and advanced it. That is a 7-yard gain. A touchback only happens if the ball lands in the end zone or goes out of bounds.
explanation.incorrect: A touchback is when the ball enters the end zone. This returner caught it at the 38 and ran it to the 45, so it is a 7-yard return.

payload.prompt: Match the kickoff outcome to where the ball ended up.

pairs.definition: The returner catches the kick and advances it before being tackled.
The ball enters the end zone or goes out of bounds; the receiving team gets the ball at the 35.
Where the kicking team lines up before the kick, at the opponent's 40-yard line.

explanation.summary: A return is when the ball is fielded and advanced. A touchback ends the play in the end zone. The setup zone is where the kicking team begins.
explanation.sayThisLine: He brought it back out of the end zone, so no touchback.

lessons.title: Fair catch and returns
lessons.objective: You can say when a fair catch is smart.

payload.prompt: Returner waves his arm at the kick, then catches it and runs.

scene.alt: A football play showing a returner waving and then attempting to run with the kickoff.

choices.label: Illegal, it is a fair catch

explanation.correct: Once he waves for a fair catch, he cannot run. The play ends where he catches it. He chose safety over yards.
explanation.incorrect: A fair catch signal means he cannot advance. Waving committed him to catching it in place.

payload.prompt: The kick is spiraling high into the air. Call fair catch or let it bounce?

situation.narrative: Your team is up by three with two minutes left. The opposing kicker just sent a long one floating down from above.

facts.label: Ball location
facts.value: At the 20-yard line, still in the air

options.label: Signal fair catch
options.consequence: You secure the ball at the 20. Your offense runs out the clock and you win.
considerations: You are ahead and protecting the lead

options.label: Let it bounce and return
options.consequence: The ball bounces at the 15. Your returner fumbles and they score. Game lost.
considerations: Time is already on your side

payload.expertNote: Fair catch is about field position and risk. When you are ahead, signal it and protect the ball.

payload.prompt: Where does the receiving team start if the kickoff goes out of bounds?

diagram.alt: Football field showing out-of-bounds kickoff and the receiving team taking over at the 35-yard line.

explanation.correct: Out of bounds kickoffs result in a touchback at the 35. Whether the kick goes out of bounds or the returner takes a touchback, the receiving team starts at the 35.
explanation.incorrect: An out-of-bounds kickoff is not midfield. The receiving team gets the automatic touchback at the 35-yard line.
explanation.sayThisLine: Out of bounds on the kick. Automatic touchback, they take it at the 35.

payload.prompt: Match the return scenario to the result.

pairs.definition: The returner waves his arm and the play ends where he catches it.
The ball enters the end zone; the receiving team starts at the 35-yard line.
The kick goes out of bounds and the receiving team takes it at the 35-yard line.

explanation.summary: Fair catch stops the play where caught. Touchbacks and out-of-bounds kicks both result in the 35-yard line start.
explanation.sayThisLine: He fair-caught it, so the play is dead right there.

lessons.title: Punting
lessons.objective: You can say why a punt is a weapon, not a surrender.

payload.prompt: What is the best reason to punt on fourth down?

options.text: You are giving up because you do not trust your offense
You are moving the opponent back, improving your field position
The rules require you to punt on fourth down

explanation.correct: A punt is a strategic weapon. You trade a possession for field position: the opponent now starts farther away. Even a 30-yard net punt gains you 40 yards of distance.
explanation.incorrect: A punt is not surrender, it is math. By moving the opponent back and changing field position, you gain a defensive advantage. It is a smart choice on short yardage far from the end zone.

payload.prompt: Your team punts from your own 30. The ball travels 50 yards, returner brings it back 5. Net distance?

explanation.correct: Fifty yards minus five yards of return equals 45 yards net. That moves the opponent from the opponent's 20-yard line back to the 20, gaining you a full 20 yards of field position.
explanation.incorrect: Calculate hang time and return: 50 yards of travel minus 5 yards of return equals 45 yards net distance.

payload.prompt: Punter aims for the opponent's sideline at their 5-yard line.

scene.alt: A football field showing a punt aimed at the opponent's sideline near the goal line.

explanation.correct: A coffin-corner punt lands out of bounds near the goal line, pinning the opponent deep in their own territory. It is a great kick and hard to execute.
explanation.incorrect: A coffin corner is a punt that goes out of bounds near the opponent's goal line, giving them poor field position. A touchback is only if the ball lands in the end zone.

payload.prompt: Match the punt outcome to the result.

pairs.definition: The ball travels far downfield; great field position for the defense.
Punt out of bounds near the goal line, pinning the opponent deep.
The ball enters the end zone, and the receiving team takes over at the 20-yard line.

explanation.summary: Long punts are powerful weapons. Coffin corners are precision kicks. Touchbacks give the opponent decent field position.
explanation.sayThisLine: That coffin-corner punt pinned them at the five.

lessons.title: Field goals
lessons.objective: You can guess whether a kick is in range.

payload.prompt: Your offense is at the opponent's 30-yard line. How long is the field goal attempt?

explanation.correct: From the 30-yard line, add about 17 yards for the distance from the goal line to the uprights and the snap depth. 30 plus 17 equals a 47-yard attempt. Most kickers make 85 percent of these.
explanation.incorrect: Field-goal range is roughly the yard line plus 17 yards. From the 30, that is 47 yards. A long kick, but within range for most NFL kickers.

payload.prompt: Offense at the opponent's 40-yard line on fourth and four.

scene.alt: Football scenario showing fourth down decision at the opponent's 40-yard line.

explanation.correct: From the 40, it is a 57-yard attempt. That is near the limit even for strong-legged kickers. You have a 40-50 percent chance. Going for it is riskier on fourth and four.
explanation.incorrect: From the 40, kicking a field goal is the conservative play. A 57-yard attempt is long but possible. Fourth and four is too far to reliably convert.

payload.prompt: After a touchdown, how far is the extra-point kick?

options.text: 20 yards from the goal line
33 yards (snapped from the 15-yard line)
It varies based on the touchdown location

explanation.correct: The extra-point kick is snapped from the 15-yard line, making it roughly a 33-yard attempt. Most kickers make 95 percent of these. It is a chip shot.
explanation.incorrect: The extra-point attempt is snapped from the 15, which is 33 yards out (including snap depth and holder distance). It is almost automatic.

payload.prompt: Your kicker is very inconsistent beyond 45 yards. Take a field goal attempt?

situation.narrative: You are down 6 with 30 seconds left. Your offense just reached the opponent's 50-yard line.

options.label: Attempt the 67-yard field goal
options.consequence: The kick is short and falls incomplete. Game over. You lost by 6.
considerations: You cannot get the ball back

options.label: Go for the touchdown
options.consequence: You have one play to score 6 points. It is a long shot, but it is your only chance.
considerations: A field goal is not enough
Your kicker cannot make this kick

payload.expertNote: A field goal attempt your kicker will miss is not a good option. Long shots require desperation, and down 6 with seconds left is it.

lessons.title: The onside kick
lessons.objective: You can explain the onside kick and the 2026 change.

payload.prompt: What is an onside kick?

options.text: A short kick the kicking team tries to recover for a second possession
A kick that stays in bounds for the entire flight
A penalty for kicking out of bounds

explanation.correct: An onside kick is a short kick (usually under 20 yards) where the kicking team tries to recover it before the receiving team. It is a desperation play when you need the ball back quickly.
explanation.incorrect: An onside kick is intentionally short, meant for the kicking team to recover. It is legal and used in certain situations: down late in the fourth quarter or after a score.

statement.speaker: Announcer
statement.text: In 2026, the kicking team can declare an onside kick at any time without surprising the receiving team.

payload.question: What changed from before?

options.text: Onside kicks are now legal all the time, not just in specific situations
The receiving team must stand still during an onside kick
Onside kicks must travel exactly 10 yards
The kicking team gets two onside kicks per game

payload.translation: Previously, onside kicks were a surprise tactic. Now the kicking team can declare one beforehand, and the receiving team lines up five players on the restraining line.

followUps.line: When would you want an onside kick?
followUps.why: Tests whether you understand field situations where recovering the ball matters more than field position.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Onside kicks are rare and desperate. Ask yourself: do we need the ball now more than we fear giving up field position?

payload.prompt: Onside kick bounces to a kicking-team player at the 48-yard line. Receiving team player was at the 47.

scene.alt: Football play showing an onside kick recovery with both teams converging on the ball.

explanation.correct: The kicking-team player got there first and recovered. They take over on offense. That is the whole point of an onside kick: surprise recovery.
explanation.incorrect: The kicking-team player reached the ball first. That is a recovery and the kicking team gets a new drive. Onside kicks are all or nothing.

payload.prompt: Match the kick type to when it is used.

pairs.definition: A short kick the kicking team tries to recover, used when desperately needing the ball back.
A long kick from the 40-yard line to the receiving team at the 35, used to start a half or after a score.
A punt aimed out of bounds near the goal line to pin the opponent deep.

explanation.summary: Onside is short and desperate. Standard kickoffs are the norm. Coffin corners are punts, not kicks.
explanation.sayThisLine: That was an onside kick, they are trying to recover it.

lessons.title: Special teams talk
lessons.objective: You can hear a special teams complaint and translate it.

statement.speaker: Coach
statement.text: Our hang time stinks. The returner had too much time.

payload.question: What is he upset about?

options.text: The kicker did not give the special teams coverage time to get downfield
The returner took too long to decide
The game is too long
The team waited too long to call timeout

payload.translation: Hang time is how long the ball stays in the air. Short hang time means the returning team gets more time and space to run. The kicker should kick higher.

followUps.line: How do you improve hang time?
followUps.why: Tests whether you know it is a kicking technique, not a coverage issue alone.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Special teams is underrated. Ask: Did the kick give us time or did the return look easy?

payload.title: Special teams moment
payload.setting: Your friend texts you about a terrible return on a big third-quarter kickoff.

exchanges.theirMessage: Did you see that kickoff return? He fumbled at the 30. Now we are in field goal range.

replies.text: Yeah, that fumble cost us the field position we had. What was he thinking?
replies.theirResponse: Exactly! The returner got hit and just lost it.
replies.coachNote: You listened to what she said and stayed focused on the fumble, not blaming the player.

replies.text: That returner is terrible. You should bench him.
replies.theirResponse: I mean, one mistake. He usually brings them back.
replies.coachNote: Overreacting to one play loses you trust. Every player has a bad moment.

replies.text: That is what you get with the new kickoff.
replies.theirResponse: That is not on the kickoff rule, that is on the returner.
replies.coachNote: True, but it missed her point about field position loss. Listen first.

exchanges.theirMessage: Yeah. And now they kicked a field goal. We were up three and now it is down to six.

replies.text: That fumble changed the whole drive. Is he the backup returner or the starter?
replies.theirResponse: He is the starter. Not sure what happened to him today.
replies.coachNote: You asked a genuine question that invited her to talk more, instead of just agreeing.

replies.text: Yeah, special teams lost this game.
replies.theirResponse: It is the third quarter. Long way to go.
replies.coachNote: The game is far from over. Do not write off the whole game yet.

replies.text: We need to go for it on our next drive. No kicking.
replies.theirResponse: That is not how football works. We cannot avoid field goals.
replies.coachNote: Reacting with a plan makes sense, but be open to her take too.

payload.closingNote: Special teams decide close games. One fumble or a great return flips momentum.

payload.prompt: What is special teams?

options.text: The offense and defense when they are performing well
Kickoffs, punts, field goals and returns: the third phase of the game
Only the players who are exceptional athletes

explanation.correct: Special teams is the third phase: kickoffs, punts, field goals, PATs and returns. It decides more games than people realize, especially close ones.
explanation.incorrect: Special teams is a whole phase of the game with its own coaches, players and schemes. It includes kickers, punters, long snappers and returners.

payload.prompt: Punt comes down high at midfield. Fair catch or field return?

situation.narrative: Your team is down 7 with four minutes left. The punt hangs up for almost four seconds.

options.label: Field return
options.consequence: Your returner breaks one for 15 yards and you are at the opponent's 35. You can score now.

options.label: Fair catch
options.consequence: You secure it at midfield. Four minutes is enough, but you lose a chance for a big return.
considerations: Midfield is a reasonable starting spot

payload.expertNote: Down 7 with time left, field returns are worth the risk at midfield. A fair catch at the 50 is safe but wastes time you need.
